# hackerscad for agents

hackerscad builds CAD models from .hcad files, a sandboxed subset of D.
Typical loop: read this reference, write a model, call hcad_render to get
dimensions and pictures, compare them with the request, fix, then export.

## Rules that avoid most mistakes
- Every exported body is a function marked @part that takes no arguments and
  returns a Solid, with the annotation on its own line:
      @part("steelblue")
      Solid body() { ... }
- Reference objects (the shaft a knob fits on, the phone a stand holds) are
  parts too, see-through and not exported, so the fit can be checked:
      @part("slategray", alpha: 0.35, export: false)
  Tag the faces of the part that touch the object (rest, grip) and check the
  fit on them.
- Lengths: write units (60.mm, 2.5.cm, 1.inch). Bare numbers passed to
  geometry are millimetres. Never add a bare number to a length (60.mm + 5 is
  an error; write 60.mm + 5.mm, or d.to!double for the bare number a length
  stands for in this file). Vectors too: write the unit on every number,
  for clarity (vec(6.25.mm, 31.5.mm)); a vector of bare numbers and one of
  lengths do not add (vec(1, 2) + vec(1.mm, 2.mm) is an error). Your own
  functions take Length parameters
  (Solid peg(Length d) …): a bare number passes as mm, a @param as it is,
  no .to!double.
- Angles: rotate(z: 45) uses degrees; 30.deg is explicit.
- A number takes its unit after a dot: 8.2.mm, not 8.2mm (in -D too).
  There is no cast: x.to!int, x.to!double, round(x), floor(x), ceil(x).
- Primitives stand on the XY plane and are centred in X and Y:
  box(x, y, z) spans z = 0 .. z; cylinder(r: or d:, h:) also; center: true
  centres in Z. sphere(r) is centred on the origin.
- Booleans: a + b (union), a - b (difference), a & b (intersection).
- Place parts relative to each other instead of computing coordinates:
  lid.nextTo(body, X, gap: 10.mm), cap.on(body).
  To put a part where another part has a place for it (a pin in a hole, a
  part on a mount), tag that place where it is made: a point or the hole's
  circle in the sketch (c.addTag("pivot")), or on the solid (b.addTag("pin",
  at: vec(…))); then part.placeOn(body.frame("pivot")), and body.point("pin")
  or body.axis("pivot") for sizes. They follow the body through every turn
  and cut: no coordinates to work out again.
- Fillets, chamfers and shells take selectors, evaluated on the solid they
  apply to: .fillet(edges.parallel(Z), r: 3.mm),
  .chamfer(edges.filter(e => e.mid.z > 5.mm), d: 1.mm),
  .shell(open: faces.top, thickness: 2.mm). Apply fillets before shell and
  before cutting holes; a fillet radius must be smaller than the faces next
  to the edge. When one fails, its error names the edges that fail and, when
  that is why, the face beside them too narrow for the size (round before
  the cut that narrows it, or make the size smaller).
- To round or chamfer the edges a cut left behind, select them by provenance:
  .fillet(edges.between(faces.from(holes), faces.top), r: 0.5.mm).
- Select by provenance, not by position: edges.between(faces.from(upright),
  faces.from(foot)) follows the @params, a filter on e.mid.z does not.
  faces.top is the highest face (after an upright with a round top is
  added, that top, no longer the foot's); faces.normal(Z) also takes
  curved faces facing up on the whole (a dome); faces.from(foot)
  has neither problem, and a frame can be taken on the solid before
  (foot.frame(faces.top)). edges.chain(edges.…) takes a curved outline
  made of many pieces whole (the edges running on without a corner),
  edges.loop(faces.top) a face's rim without its holes; a profile's
  p.outer, p.holes and p.pieces give its outline, its holes and its
  regions.
- Where you can, avoid fixed coordinates and selectors by position (a filter
  on e.mid.z, on a face's area or centre): they stop matching when a size
  changes. Prefer what follows the model, provenance or a tag; when no plain
  selector picks a face, tag it rather than filter for it. Fixed coordinates
  are right where the place itself is fixed (a hole measured on the real
  part).
  Tag a face you will come back to, where it is made: b.faces.top.addTag("lid")
  (it changes b and gives it back, so box(…).faces.top.addTag("lid") works in
  a chain), then faces.tagged("lid") wherever the part was turned or placed
  since; a tool tagged recursive (drill.addTag("bore", recursive: true))
  tags the wall it cuts. Name what a face does (lid, mount, seat, grip), not
  where it is; tag only what a later step uses, and in a library the faces
  its users need. A tag not found: the error lists the tags there are; fix
  the name rather than switching to a selector by position.
  The libraries tag what you come back to (hardware.bore, gears.axis,
  hinges.pin, enclosures.rim…: the list is in hcad docs): use them rather
  than selecting those faces again; two of a kind in one part: tag each
  whole with a name of yours and chain, faces.tagged("left").tagged("hinges.pin").
- Cut with planes: body.halves(body.plane(faces.top).offset(-10.mm)) gives
  .above and .below; body.split(plane) the pieces on both sides; s.pieces
  lists separate bodies, ordered along X, Y, Z.
- Profiles: rect, circle, ellipse, polygon, slot, teardrop (the shapes of a
  sketch, same names and arguments, centred on the origin unless given a
  point: rect(40.mm, 20.mm, corner: 3.mm), rect(p, q), circle(c, d: 5.mm),
  rect(center: vec(15.4, 3.3), w: 5.6.mm, h: 14.mm, angle: 45.deg) (a
  rotated one, round a point),
  polygon(6, d: 13.mm, fit: "sides"), slot(p, q, w: 6.mm)), polygon(points),
  text; combined with + - &, moved, turned, scaled, mirrored like solids,
  .round(r), .offset(d); turn them into solids with .extrude(h) or
  .revolve(axis: Y). A prism along X or Y: .extrude(h, along: Y) (the
  profile's x along X, its y up Z, towards +Y; along: X its x along Y,
  towards +X; a negative h the other way); taper: 3.deg narrows the solid
  and widens its holes going away from the profile, whichever way it goes
  (a negative taper widens it and narrows the holes). shear: vec(dx, dy)
  moves the top sideways from the bottom, the sides leaning straight: an
  oblique prism (a blade's bevel; a section's outline that moves the same
  way at every level). A profile in another
  plane (a section, one turned or moved, one drawn on a face) extrudes
  across its own plane, from where it lies. On a face:
  body.extrude(profile, on: frame, depth:) adds, body.cut(profile, on:
  frame, depth: | through: true) removes.
  Stand a profile up with p.across(X) or across(Y) (as extrude(along:)
  does), not with rotate: loft([a.across(X), b.across(X).move(x: 20.mm)])
  runs along X.
- Sweeps and lofts: circle(d: 4.mm).sweep(path([vec(0, 0, 0), vec(0, 0, 30),
  vec(30, 0, 30)])), circle(d: 1.mm).sweep(helix(r: 5.mm, pitch: 2.mm,
  height: 20.mm), frenet: true), loft([circle(r: 20), rect(25).move(z: 40)]).
  A path to sweep along: drawn in a sketch (s.path; the sketch's
  constraints hold it), along a solid's edges
  (body.path(edges.loop(faces.top))), with bent corners (path(points,
  bend: 5.mm) for tubes and wires), or from two views (path(top.path,
  front.path): a handle drawn from above on XY and from the front on XZ).
  How the profile turns about the path: up: Z for a road that does not
  bank, guide: rail where up fails (a path going vertical), twist: t =>
  angle for a roll that varies; never two of them.
- Surfaces: a curve swept (path([vec(-8.mm, 0), vec(8.mm, 0)])
  .sweep(route)) or paths lofted make a Surface: body.split(surface) cuts
  a solid along it (a tube split lengthwise by a ribbon swept along its
  own path), pieces.push(from: surface, by:) opens them, surface.thicken(t)
  and sew([surfaces, caps]) make solids. A part cannot be a surface.
- Exact 2D outlines with dimensions: auto s = sketch(); points, lines, arcs,
  circles, ellipses, splines (s.spline([p, q, r]): a smooth curve through
  points, closed: true a loop of its own) and shapes (s.rect, s.polygon(c,
  6, d:, fit: "sides"), s.slot, s.teardrop), then constraints (horizontal, vertical, length,
  distance, angle, tangent, on, equal, concentric…) and s.profile, to
  extrude or revolve. construction: true on any of them makes a guide to
  constrain to, never part of the profile. The profile fills what lies
  inside an odd number of loops: a loop in a loop is a hole, and where
  two loops overlap so is the overlap; s.fill(at) makes the area holding
  at full, s.fill(at, full: false) empty.
  Prefer a sketch over unions and differences of boxes and cylinders for
  the outline of a prismatic part (built from flat outlines, extruded,
  revolved and cut: a bracket, a plate, a case, a holder, a knob, a cam, a
  gasket, a clip; not a sculpted shape like a figurine), with the sizes
  given or estimated (estimated ones become @params): write each dimension
  as a constraint, aim for s.dof == 0 (a warning lists what is left free),
  then add 3D features (holes, fillets, shells) to the extruded solid. A
  profile made of more than three shapes, moved by sizes worked out by
  hand, or rounded with .offset(r).offset(-r) is an outline that wants a
  sketch: it reads as its dimensions, keeps its tangents when a @param
  changes, and its edges take fillets. One shape alone can stay one line
  (rect(40.mm, 20.mm, corner: 3.mm)); in a sketch (s.rect) its sizes
  become dimensions the user changes with a click in the window. Examples
  below: the medal (a first sketch, step by step), the pillow block (a
  part from five sketches on five surfaces) and the carlo library (a clip
  drawn with tangent arcs, a loop and if/else).
- To build on a face, take its frame and place parts built on XY (Z up):
  cylinder(d: 8.mm, h: 5.mm).placeOn(body.frame(faces.top).at(x: 10.mm)).
- To draw an outline on a face, measured from the part's own edges, sketch
  there: auto s = body.sketch(faces.top); its edges are references in
  s.edges (the lowest first, counter-clockwise: bottom, right, top, left on
  a rectangular face), s.origin is its centre, s.project(edges.…) flattens
  other edges onto it (a hole's rim below). Constrain the new geometry to
  them (s.distance(p, s.edges[0], 3.mm)), then body.cut(s.profile, depth:)
  or body.extrude(s.profile, depth:): the profile knows its face, no on:.
  In the window: hcad_gui_feature with action sketch on a flat face.
- Axes and planes anywhere: rotate(90.deg, axis: body.axis(edges.filter(e =>
  e.isCircle && e.radius == 3.mm))), s.mirror(plane(origin: vec(10, 0, 0),
  normal: X)), plane(p1, p2, p3), plane(axis, point). XY, XZ and YZ face
  the Top, Front and Right views (XZ's normal is -Y): a sketch on XZ reads
  as the Front view shows it. A plane kept in a variable shows in the
  window's planes, named after it; body.plane(faces.top, faces.bottom) is
  halfway between two parallel faces.
- Existing parts: load("part.stl"/".obj"/".ply"/".3mf"/".glb"/".step", scale: 1) gives a
  solid to modify (glTF is turned from metres and Y up to mm and Z up; repair:
  true mends a scan's doubled walls and sheets that touch); text("LABEL", size: 4.mm).centered centres a profile for engraving.
- When asked to copy lettering from a photo, a drawing or a model: if the
  font cannot be recognised, or text() does not have it (it uses the fonts
  installed), ask the user before going on, offering a similar installed
  font (name it), or tracing the letters as a sketch (lines and arcs sized
  from the picture), or load("letters.svg") if they can give a vector
  tracing; never swap the font before the user has chosen (saying so
  afterwards is not enough). Working with no one to ask (a task run on its
  own): trace the letters as a sketch, and say so in the report. Logos, engraved or hand-drawn
  lettering are traced as a sketch. Lettering on a mesh or STEP to copy
  needs no question: its exact shape is there (see Remodelling a mesh).
- Constants are immutable; module-level values cannot be modified.
- Solids, profiles and paths are values, not references: b.move(x: 5.mm);
  alone changes nothing (warning E0208), write b = b.move(x: 5.mm); only
  addTag, removeTag and clearTags change the solid they are called on.
- Expose the dimensions a user may want to change as parameters:
      @param("Outer width", min: 20.mm, max: 200.mm)
      immutable width = 60.mm;
  and put requirements in unittest blocks:
  unittest { assert(body.bbox.size.z <= 40.mm, "must fit in the drawer"); }
- Use the libraries instead of modelling common parts by hand: import std;
  gives them all (import std.hardware : M3, hole; only those names).
  std.hardware: M3.clearance, M3.tap, screw(M3, 20.mm), nut(M3),
  hole(M3, 5.mm, "counterbore"|"insert"|…);
  std.threads (threadedRod, tappedHole); std.gears (spurGear, rack,
  centerDistance); std.hinges (hinge(…).fixed/.moving, print in place);
  std.snaps (snapHook, snapSlot); std.enclosures (roundedBox, tray,
  enclosure(vec(x, y, z)).base/.lid); std.joints (splitJoint(body,
  plane, kind: "dovetail"|"dowels"|…).a/.b for a part longer than the bed,
  .loose/.print the wedge or dowels in place and laid flat; splitFlat
  for two halves printed on their cut faces, joinParts(a, b, plane));
  std.molds (mold(part, plane).aPrint/.bPrint); std.flex (kerf(body, zone)
  to make it bend; hinges also has pinHinge, snapHinge, livingHinge).
  Built in: region.tiles(kind: "hex"|"voronoi"|…) fills a profile with
  cells, body.knurl(face) raises a grip, body.cut(profile, wrap: face,
  depth:) lays a profile on a curved face.
- Before modelling anything common by hand (a teardrop, a screw hole, a
  nut trap, a thread, a slot, a rounded box), look for it: hcad_docs with
  a topic, or format: cheatsheet (every function in one line); write your
  own only when nothing fits.
- Functions are ordinary arguments: xs.map(x => x * 2), xs.filter(f).
- Your own modules: import parts.bracket; is parts/bracket.hcad next to the
  model; import pizza; is pizza.hcad or pizza/package.hcad (which can
  public import its modules), also from the personal library folder.
- Strings interpolate: writeln("volume: $(body.volume)"); text("…", size:)
  is a 2D text profile, not a string function.
- Errors come with a line, a column and often a suggestion: apply it.
- Technical drawings: a function marked @drawing returns drawing(title: …),
  filled with d.standardViews(part) (views, overall dimensions, hole
  callouts) and d.section(part, XZ, label: "A"); export it as .pdf/.svg/.dxf.
- Keep models quick to evaluate: text cut into curved faces and threads take
  seconds; prefer text in relief as a separate part, and plain holes or
  heat-set inserts (hole(M3, d, "insert")) or ribs the screw cuts its
  thread into (hole(M3, d, "ribs")) to modelled threads under M5.
- Style: annotations (@param, @preset, @part, @drawing) go on their own line above
  the declaration, several per line when short; chains break before each
  call, the line starting with the dot; lines short (the editor shows about
  56 characters at its default width); an empty line above each comment
  (not right after { or another comment); comments say why.
- For an example, a trial or an explanation that needs some object to work
  on (to move, cut, place, measure), use Carlo, the mascot clip: import
  std; then carlo(), and call it Carlo (always the same, recognisable,
  small and quick to evaluate). Not instead of an object the
  request names (the phone, the shaft): model that one.

## Sketches: habits
- Pin one point (fixed: true) or the outline floats.
- A distance is never negative: which side comes from where the points are
  drawn; draw them roughly where they go.
- Guides that are not part of the outline: construction: true lines and
  circles (a diagonal whose midpoint is the centre, a circle to inscribe in).
- s.on(shape, circle) puts every corner of a rect/polygon on a circle,
  s.tangent(shape, circle) every side touching it; polygon(…, fit: "sides")
  sizes it across the flats (a nut's spanner size).
- A profile is a flat closed shape with its holes. One outline told by its
  sizes and relations: a sketch. Overlapping shapes, an offset outline, text
  or an SVG on a shape: profile operations (+ - &, .offset). They mix:
  s.profile + circle(d: 5.mm).
- Tag the lines and circles whose faces a later step works on (a flank for a
  label, a hole's wall to thread): sides[1].addTag("flank"), then
  faces.tagged("flank") on the solid. It holds when the profile is extruded
  or revolved as the sketch gives it (moved or turned first is fine), not
  when it is joined to another profile, tapered or swept first.

## Prismatic parts and 3D printing
- A prismatic part: its outline as a sketch from the drawing's dimensions,
  extruded or revolved; then fillets and chamfers; then holes (hardware:
  hole(M3, depth, "clearance" | "tap" | "insert" | "ribs" | "counterbore" |
  "countersink")); then check.
- Then build in steps, as on a machine: each further feature (a boss, a
  pocket, a slot, a rib, a step) starts from a face and is extruded from
  it or cut into it; on the faces it makes, again. Not one profile with
  everything at once: each step reads as what it does, and follows its
  face when a @param moves it. A feature of one shape at a place you know
  is one profile on the face: body.cut(circle(d: 6.mm), on:
  body.frame(faces.top), depth: 3.mm), body.extrude(rect(10.mm, 4.mm),
  on: …). A sketch on the face, body.sketch(faces.…), when its outline has
  several shapes or relations (tangent, equal), or its place is measured
  from the face's edges. A feature with a tool of its own takes that tool:
  hole() for a screw, shell for thin walls, a loop for a pattern, a
  library part, a loft or sweep for a shape that changes along its length.
  Example: the pillow block.
- Fits: ask how it will be made (FDM, resin, machined) before choosing
  clearances; for FDM about 0.2–0.3 mm for a sliding fit, press fits from a
  test print. Put clearances in @params.
- Holes across a wall that will print sideways: teardrop(d:) with the point
  up (flat: true cuts the point). Say how the part is meant to print, and
  lay it so (its largest flat face on the ground); look at --printability.

## Copying a real part, or building onto one
- From a photo or a real object to copy or build onto (not a mesh or STEP:
  those have the sizes, see below), your first reply is
  the questions, before writing any code or touching the user's window
  (no hcad_gui_new, no hcad_gui_edit), even when the user says "make it"
  without giving sizes. In one message: the sizes to measure (below), the
  font if there is lettering, and, said plainly, that any of them can be
  left: the more answered the better, the rest estimated from the photo
  (they may be off: @params to correct after a test print). Estimate only when the user answers so, or already said so in the
  request ("just estimate", "I have no caliper"). Saying at the end what
  was estimated does not replace asking.
- Do not invent shapes or sizes you are not sure of: ask. Ask in the way
  that helps: not "how big is it?" but what to measure and how ("with a
  caliper, the distance between the centres of the two holes, axis to
  axis"; "how thick is the rim at the arrow in the photo?"; "is the left
  side straight or curved?"). Number the questions, say what each size is
  for, and which sizes are critical (fits, holes) and which can be rough.
  If, once asked, the user cannot measure or asks you to estimate, say what is estimated and make those sizes
  @params to correct after a test print.
- From a photo: ask for one known size (the scale) and about the hidden
  sides; say which sizes are guessed.

## Remodelling a mesh or STEP
- The sizes are in the file: start at once, no questions. Load it as a
  see-through reference part beside the copy (@part("slategray", alpha:
  0.35, export: false) Solid original() => load("x.stl");), straightened
  if tilted (load(…).aligned).
- 1, read it: hcad_features (chamfers with their size, holes, surfaces
  turned round an axis), hcad_scan along x, y and z (the holes and pockets
  as the operations they were made with), then hcad_section at the levels
  the scans name: exact lines and arcs (region: only the outlines inside a
  rectangle, a lettering, a pocket).
- 2, build from the largest to the smallest: the outside as one outline
  per stretch, the sketch hcad_section gives at that level pasted and
  extruded; then, as for any prismatic part, the features on its faces in
  steps: one of one shape (a round hole, a rectangular pocket, a boss) is
  a profile with the sizes hcad_scan and hcad_features give (hole() when
  they name a screw size); one whose outline has several shapes, a
  section of the original parallel to that face, just inside it, its
  sketch pasted and extruded from the face or cut into it (the sketch is
  in the plane's own coordinates: extrude it along that axis from the
  face's level); the chamfers of the end faces
  before anything is cut in them; then holes, pockets and traps; last
  small chamfers, notches and lettering. Lettering (small regular grooves
  0.5 mm deep in a face are lettering, not notches): cut a section 0.25 mm
  inside the face, paste the sketch hcad_section gives with region round
  the letters (it solves as it is), extrude it 0.5 mm into the face; never
  trace by hand.
- 3, THE ROUND: after every change, hcad_review (hcad review on the
  command line). One call does it all: the distances both ways, the
  material that differs, the drawings outside and of the voids, and
  close-ups of the first entries of each, chosen and framed where they are
  in sight; it ends saying whether it is done or what comes next. It is a
  summary, the first three entries of each report; detail: true gives
  them all. Fix what the close-ups show and review again. To look at a place again after a
  change, give its point (look: [x, y, z]): entry numbers change, points
  do not. The single tools (hcad_compare, hcad_diff, hcad_lines, focus,
  view) go deeper on one place; hcad_section with compare where the
  review says, to read a shape; opaque: true draws the reference solid.
- 4, then: hcad_match (the operations one by one: a hexagon where the copy
  has a circle, a trap cut in steps, a notch for printing); hcad_lines with
  depth once the outside and the voids match; hcad_fit only to tune sizes
  of a shape already right.
- 5, done when hcad_review says so (95% or more of both surfaces within
  0.1 mm) and its close-ups show nothing worth fixing.
- 6, name the measures that matter: hcad_literals lists the numbers the
  model repeats and which sizes of the original they are (a hole's
  diameter, an axis); make those @params or named constants, use the
  names, and put the relations in unittest blocks (the rod fits its hole).
  Tag the faces that do the work (the one it rests on, a mating face, a
  screw's seat) where they are made, so the checks and later changes find
  them by name.
- What the numbers do not say: hcad_diff leaves out what is thinner than
  two cubes, and says how much it left (chamfers, lettering, notches: look
  at hcad_lines). When hcad_fit takes away little, or moves a size away
  from what an exact section measures, the shape differs, not the sizes:
  cut sections elsewhere, off the axis too (a step that drops towards the
  sides is often turned round an axis; hcad_features names it).
- Parts printed and shared online have habits to look for: notches on top
  of sideways holes, a layer closing a hole for a millimetre (printed over,
  drilled after), teardrop points cut flat at an angle that is not 45°
  (read it from the section, not teardrop()), nut traps wider at the mouth,
  0.5 mm chamfers where holes open.

## Before saying it is done
- No errors and no warnings (an under-constrained sketch's warning counts);
  the sizes match the request; reference parts fit, with no unwanted
  overlap ((a & b).volume); printability looked at if it is to be printed;
  the pictures actually looked at.
- Say what was not checked (a fit that needs a test print, a size guessed).
- Say it briefly, and name the @params the user can change to try variants.

## Showing and asking with annotations (hcad_gui_annotate)
- Use them to ask and to answer, not only words: "is this the face you
  mean?" (an arrow on it), "the wall is 0.8 mm here" (a cross and a
  label), "should the hole go here or here?" (two numbered crosses, and the
  question in the chat with the same numbers). When an answer is about a
  place on the model, show it.
- Turn and frame the view first, so it can be understood: the part of
  interest in sight, not hidden behind another, seen from a side that
  makes it recognisable, with enough around it to tell where it is on the
  part (not zoomed so close that it is unclear what it is, nor so far that
  the detail is lost); one view per question if needed. Annotations lock
  the view: frame it, then annotate.
- Unless the user asks otherwise: arrows, crosses and circles in a colour
  that stands out in that view, against the part's colour and the
  background (not the part's own colour: red or magenta on a sky-blue part,
  blue or black on a red one); short labels, off the part; few marks at a
  time, one per thing to point at.
- When the user says "here", "this", "from here to there", or asks you to
  look at the marks: read them in hcad_gui_state, not in a screenshot.
  Each point has the part, face, point in mm and selector under it; a
  point on the background has points_at, the surface the mark points at
  (ahead of an arrow, or the nearest round it) and how many pixels away;
  each mark has colour_name beside its hex (the default magenta is often
  called purple or violet). A screenshot only for what the data cannot
  tell: the shape of a line drawn by hand, a mark with nothing under it
  and no points_at. If in doubt, confirm what you understood with a mark
  of your own before changing the model.
- When they have served, clear your marks (clear: "agent", or mode: false):
  while any are there the view stays locked and changes to the model do not
  show. Do not clear the user's marks without asking.

# The `.hcad` language

A `.hcad` file is written in an **interpreted, sandboxed scripting language inspired by D**. Anyone who knows D can read it without
surprises, and its C-style syntax reads at once to anyone who has written C, Java, C# or JavaScript: braces, semicolons,
`if` and `for`, functions with typed parameters. There is no compilation step: the interpreter runs inside hackerscad and
re-evaluates a model in milliseconds.

New to it? The [tour of the language](#a-tour-of-the-language) at the end is one model that uses each
basic construct once, with comments saying what each makes appear; in the application it is under
**Examples › Language tour** (and ☰ › Language Tour).

This page lists everything in brief; the [guides by topic](GUIDES.md) explain each subject at length, with pictures.

## What stays the same as D
- **Lexical:** identifiers; numbers (`42`, `1_000`, `2.5`, `0xFF`, `2.5e3`); strings `"…"`, `` `…` ``, `r"…"` (the last two WYSIWYG as in D); comments `//`, `/* */` and nested `/+ +/`.
- **Declarations:** `immutable`, `const`, `auto`, typed variables, `struct` (fields, defaults, methods), functions (with `{ … }` or `=> expr;` bodies), `import`, `unittest`, UDAs.
- **Statements:** `if`/`else`, `foreach` (`foreach (i, x; arr)`, `foreach (i; 0 .. n)`, `foreach_reverse`), `for`, `while`, `break`, `continue`, `return`, `assert`, `switch` (with `case a, b:` and `default:`). A condition (of `if`, `while`, `&&`, `!`, `?:`, a `filter` or `any` predicate) is a `bool`, or an integer as in D (0 is false); a length, a solid or a text there is an error: compare it (`e.length > 2.mm`).
- **Assignments:** `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `~=`, `++`, `--`.
- **Expressions:**
  - D precedence, including `^^`; ternary `?:`.
  - UFCS: `x.f(y)` is `f(x, y)`.
  - Named arguments: `f(x: 1)`.
  - Lambdas: `x => e`, `(a, b) => e`, `(int x) { return x; }`.
  - Functions are ordinary arguments: `xs.map(x => x * 2)`, `xs.map(&twice)`.
  - Array literals `[1, 2]` and associative literals `["a": 1]`.
  - Slices `a[1 .. $]`, concatenation `~`, `in`.
  - Struct literals `Screw("M3", 3.mm)` or `Screw(d: 3.mm)`.
- **Paren-less calls:** a declared function whose parameters all have defaults is called when named without parentheses (`body.bbox`, `nextTo(body, …)`). Use `&f` to pass the function itself.
- **Modules:**
  - `import std;` (every built-in library at once), `import std.math;`, `import std.hardware : M3;`, `import hw = std.hardware;`, `import lib.hinges;`, `import a, b;`.
  - `lib.hinges` resolves to `lib/hinges.hcad`; a folder is a package: `import pizza;` loads `pizza.hcad`, or else `pizza/package.hcad`, whose `public import pizza.base, pizza.toppings;` makes their names visible to whoever imports `pizza` (as in D).
  - Modules are looked for in the directory of the model, then in the folders of `$HCAD_PATH`, then in the personal library folder: `~/.local/share/hackerscad/lib` on Linux (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/hackerscad/lib`), `~/Library/Application Support/hackerscad/lib` on macOS, `%APPDATA%\hackerscad\lib` on Windows. The built-in libraries are `std.hardware`, `std.gears`… (`import std;` imports them all, also as `import std : M3, hole;` or `import s = std;`; imported without `std.`, the old way, they still work with a warning, and a module of yours of that name comes first).
  - `private` symbols are not exported.

## What is different from D
- **Strings interpolate:** `"volume: $(body.volume)"` inserts the value of the expression; `\$` is a literal dollar. Backtick and `r"…"` strings are WYSIWYG and never interpolate.
- **`~` joins anything with a string:** `"side " ~ width` gives `"side 60 mm"` (in D both sides must be strings).
- **Dynamic typing with run-time checks.**
  - `auto` works everywhere.
  - Declared types (`Length h`, `Solid f()`) are checked on calls, returns and assignments, with clear errors.
  - There are no templates: functions are passed as normal arguments (`xs.filter(x => x > 0)`). `!` is only used for type conversions (`to!string`).
- **Value semantics.** Arrays, associative arrays and structs behave as values: `b = a; b[0] = 9;` does not change `a`.
  Solids, profiles, surfaces and paths too: a method gives a new one and leaves the one it is called on as it was, so `pieces[0].color("red");` alone changes nothing (a warning says so, E0208); write `pieces[0] = pieces[0].color("red");`. Only `addTag`, `removeTag` and `clearTags` change the solid they are called on (and give it back too).
- **An array literal holds one type**, as in D: `[1, "a"]` or `[1.mm, 2.deg]` is an error naming the two elements; whole and fractional numbers mix, and bare numbers with Lengths (`[1.mm, 2]`, the bare number in mm, as in `vec`).
- **Purity.**
  - Locals inside functions are mutable.
  - Module-level declarations (`immutable`, and even `auto`) are read-only and evaluated lazily, in any order. Constants use `immutable`; `enum` is reserved for enumerations.
  - Every function is therefore deterministic, and results can be cached. This is the basis of incremental regeneration.
- **Not available:** classes, pointers, `mixin`, `static if`, user templates, exceptions, `asm`, `alias`, `new`.
- **Sandbox.**
  - `load()` reads mesh, STEP and drawing (SVG, DXF) files inside the project directory only.
  - Library imports are limited to hackerscad's standard modules: `std.shapes`, `std.math`, `std.algorithm`, `std.range`, `std.conv`, `std.format`, `std.stdio`, `std.array`, and the built-in libraries (`std.hardware`, `std.threads`, `std.gears`, `std.hinges`, `std.snaps`, `std.enclosures`, `std.joints`, `std.molds`, `std.flex`, `std.carlo`; `std` is all of them).
  - Imports cannot leave the project directory or the library folder they were found in.
  - There is no file, network or process access.
  - Evaluation steps, recursion depth and array sizes are limited.
- **`writeln`** writes to hackerscad's console (and to the JSON output for agents), not to stdout. A shape is written as a short summary (`Solid 30 × 20 × 10 mm, volume 6000 mm³`, `Profile 30 × 20 mm, area 600 mm²`, `Path 82.3 mm long, open`), a selection taken from a solid with how many it selects (`faces (3)`).

## hackerscad additions
- **Units** are UFCS functions: `60.mm`, `2.5.cm`, `1.m`, `1.inch`, `45.deg`, `0.5.rad`.
  - Values carry a dimension (`Length`, `Angle`, `Area`, `Volume`), and arithmetic checks it: `Length * Length` is an `Area`, while `60.mm + 45.deg` is an error. An angle multiplied with a length, or a length divided by an angle, counts in radians as the plain ratio it is (an arc over its radius): `r * 90.deg` is the length of a quarter of a circle of radius r, a `Length`, and `arc / 90.deg` is the radius of that arc, a `Length` too (`arc / r` is a plain number, the angle in radians).
  - **Bare numbers** passed where a length is expected use the file's default unit: `mm`, or the unit set with `@unit(inch) module name;`. Values keep their unit, so libraries written with different default units combine correctly.
  - Mixing bare and dimensioned numbers in arithmetic (`60.mm + 5`) is an error. Scaling is fine (`2 * 60.mm`).
  - A dimensioned number as a bare one: `d.to!double` is the bare number that means it in this file, a length in the file's unit (millimetres, as `d / 1.mm`, or inches under `@unit(inch)`; squared for an area, cubed for a volume), an angle in degrees (as `a / 1.deg`); `d.to!int` the same when it is whole. To mix it with bare numbers: `c.y + d.to!double / 2`, or give the other side its unit: `vec(6.25.mm, 31.5.mm)`.
  - Bare angles passed to features (`rotate(z: 45)`) are degrees. `sin`/`cos` take radians for bare numbers, as in D.
- **Vectors:** `vec(10.mm, 5.mm)`, `vec(x, y, z)`, with `.x .y .z .xy .length .normalized`, `dot`, `cross`, `distance`. Vectors compare with a small tolerance.
- **Directions:** `X`, `Y`, `Z`, `-X`…
- **`@param("description", min:, max:, step:, choices:)`** above **`immutable name = default;`** declares a parameter. It can be overridden from the GUI, from the CLI (`-D name=80.mm`, or `-D name=80` in the model unit; for a string, `-D style=square` is the word itself when it names nothing, else quote it: `-D style='"square"'`) and by agents, and is checked against its limits.
- **`@preset("name", value)`** on a parameter gives its value in a named preset (`--preset name`, or the preset menu in the GUI). A preset is the set of values declared under its name; parameters without a value for it keep their default.
  - Parameters never change during an evaluation: their value is decided beforehand, from default, then preset, then explicit override.
  - Like a configuration table: every parameter is a column, every preset a row.
- **`@part("colour")`** above **`Solid name() { … }`** declares an exported body: a separate object in 3MF, a separate named body in STEP, its own file in a zip of STLs (`name.stl`; a lone `.stl` takes one part). A part is evaluated once per run even when other parts refer to it. Without a colour a part is Sky Pop (`#0FC3F2`). `@part("slategray", alpha: 0.35)` makes it see-through; `export: false` makes it a reference part (a shaft, a board, the object a holder is for): drawn in the view and in PNGs, left out of STL, 3MF and STEP. `name: "Tank"` is the part's name in exported files (object, body and file names) instead of the function's; two parts cannot share one.
- **`@parts`** above a function makes **a part of each separate body** it returns: of a `Solid` (two halves of a cut, copies that do not touch, the objects of a loaded 3MF) or of each element of a `Solid[]`. The parts are named after the function with a number, `jaws1`, `jaws2`… (just `jaws` when there is one), in the order of `.pieces` (along X, then Y, then Z); how many there are comes from the evaluation, so a parameter can change it. It takes what `@part` takes, plus `varied: true`, which gives the pieces colours that tell apart (the first in the part's colour). A piece coloured on its own (`pieces[1] = pieces[1].color("Blue Pop");`, what the menu's Colour writes on a piece) keeps its colour; the others take the annotation's. A solid in a `Solid[]` made of several bodies stays one part. An empty `Solid[]` makes no part: a part to choose with a parameter, `@parts Solid[] lid() => withLid ? [makeLid()] : [];`. `@part` on a function returning a `Solid[]` is an error that points at `@parts`; on a `Solid` of several bodies it is one part (one object in 3MF).
  ```d
  import std;   // Carlo, the mascot clip, is in it: an object to try things on

  immutable cutPlane = plane(origin: vec(10, 0, 0), normal: X);

  @parts(varied: true)
  Solid[] pieces() => carlo().split(cutPlane);    // pieces1, pieces2, pieces3: the plane crosses the slot

  @parts("Yellow Pop")
  Solid jaws() => carlo().halves(cutPlane).above; // jaws1, jaws2: the side above is two bodies
  ```
- **Colours** are CSS names (`"steelblue"`), hackerscad's own bright colours, alike in brightness under the view's light and offered by the 3D view's right-click menu (`"Sky Pop"` — the default —, `"Blue Pop"`, `"Cyan Pop"`, `"Violet Pop"`, `"Pink Pop"`, `"Rose Pop"`, `"Red Pop"`, `"Orange Pop"`, `"Yellow Pop"`, `"White Pop"`, `"Gray Pop"`: with the space, `"Pink Pop"` is not the web's `"pink"`), `"#RRGGBB"`, `"#RRGGBBAA"` (the last byte is the opacity) or `rgb(r, g, b)` with 0…255 channels, `rgb(r, g, b, alpha: 0.5)`. `solid.color("orange", alpha: 0.5)` works too.
- **`unittest { assert(…); }`** blocks are design checks. They run after evaluation; a failure does not discard the geometry, but is reported in the GUI, the CLI and to agents. `hcad check`, `hcad render` and the exports run them every time; the window runs them when asked (F5, the bug button over the console, `hcad_gui_test` for agents) and before an export, not at every change.
- **Solids and booleans:**
  - `a + b` union, `a - b` difference, `a & b` intersection; `s += x` inside functions.
  - `hull(a, b, …)` or `hull([a, b, …])`: the smallest convex shape around solids and profiles (two spheres make a capsule, four cylinders a plate with round corners); profiles in one plane give a profile, `hull(circle(r: 4.mm), circle(r: 4.mm).move(x: 20.mm))` a slot. Curved surfaces become flat facets within 0.05 mm. Their flat faces the hull lies on keep their tags. `hull(a, b, grow: 2.mm)` is the hull grown that much all round, its edges and corners rounded (at most 2% farther, never nearer): a case round what it holds, quicker and surer than `.offset` on a hull of thousands of faces.
  - `minkowski(a, b)`: `a` moved by every point of `b`. With a sphere (a circle for profiles) it rounds every edge and corner exactly, like `s.offset(r)`; with another convex shape (a box, a cylinder) it is made of flat facets, and one of the two shapes must be convex. Their flat faces, moved out, keep their tags; `a`'s own tags and references stay.
  - `s.offset(d)` grows a solid by `d` (or shrinks it, `d` negative), round where it turns; `sharp: true` moves its faces and extends them until they meet, the edges staying sharp (a box stays a box). Holes it grows over (a hole's radius or more) close up: they are filled first.
- **Printing:** `teardrop(d: 5.mm)` (in a sketch `s.teardrop(c, d: 5.mm)`) is a round hole with a 45° point towards +Y: cut on a wall (`carlo().cut(teardrop(d: 3.4.mm), on: faces.farthest(-Y), through: true)`) the point is up and the hole prints without supports (`angle:` another point, `flat: true` cuts it at the circle's top). `faces.overhanging()` selects the faces facing down more steeply than 45° from a wall (`faces.overhanging(60.deg)` another angle; faces resting on the bed are not counted), `s.overhangs(45.deg)` is their area and `s.thinWalls(0.8.mm)` the surface over walls thinner than that: `assert(part.thinWalls == 0.mm ^^ 2)` in a unittest keeps a model printable. The Printability check box of the display menu marks both on the model.
- **Profiles from solids:** `s.section(XZ)` (any plane: `s.section(s.plane(faces.top).offset(-2.mm))`) is the cut of the solid by the plane, a profile lying in it; `s.projection` is the solid's shadow seen from above, a profile on XY, and `s.projection(XZ)` its shadow on any plane, cast along the plane's normal (curved surfaces within 0.02 mm; its outline read back as lines, arcs and circles, so that it extrudes and sweeps as fast as one drawn). Both can be extruded, offset, combined like any profile.
- **Mass:** `s.centroid` is the centre of mass; `s.mass(density: 1.24)` the mass in grams for a density in g/cm³ (PLA 1.24, PETG 1.27, ABS 1.04, aluminium 2.70, steel 7.85); `s.inertia(density: 1.24)` the principal moments of inertia about the centre of mass, ascending, in g·mm².
  - `a - [b, c, …]` takes every solid of the list away from `a` at once: much quicker than one at a time (400 holes in a plate: 0.7 s, against 16 s in a loop).
  - `Solid.init` is the empty solid; `Solid all;` and `Profile all;` start empty, to add to in a loop. `solids.sum` and `fuse(…)` unite arrays. A `@part` that returns `Solid.nothing` is no part this time (`return solid ? Solid.nothing : cap();`: a lid left out by a parameter); one left empty otherwise (a cut that took it all, a loop that added nothing) is an error, as it is most likely a mistake.
- **Math** (with `import std.math`): `sqrt`, `abs`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan` (angles; bare numbers are radians), `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2(y, x)`, `pow(x, y)` (as `x ^^ y`: a length squared is an area), `exp`, `log(x)` and `log(x, base)`, `log10`, `log2`, `hypot(a, b)`, `sign`, `min`, `max`, `clamp(v, lo, hi)`, `lerp(a, b, t)` (numbers, lengths or vectors), and `PI`, `E`.
- **Primitives** stand on the XY plane, centred in X and Y; `center: true` centres them in Z too. Spheres are centred.
  - `box(x, y, z)`, `cylinder(r | d, h)`, `cone(r1 | d1, r2 | d2, h)`, `sphere(r | d)`, `torus(major, minor)` (round Z, centred on the origin: major to the middle of the tube, minor its radius).
- **Profiles** (2D shapes on the XY plane, type `Profile`):
  - The shapes are those of a sketch (below), with the same names and arguments: a profile's shape is a one-shape sketch with everything given, centred on the origin unless a point is given (a vector, `vec(10, 5)` or `[10, 5]`). `rect(w, h)` (`rect(20.mm)`, a square), `rect(p, q)` (two opposite corners), `rect(p, w:, h:)` (from its lower left corner) or `rect(center: c, w:, h:)`, with `angle: 30.deg` (rotated about its centre, its first side that far from X: a slanted rectangle anywhere is `rect(center: vec(15.4, 3.3), w: 5.6.mm, h: 14.mm, angle: 45.deg)`) and `corner: 3.mm` (the four corners rounded); `circle(r | d)` or `circle(c, r | d)`; `ellipse(rx, ry)` or `ellipse(c, rx:, ry:)`, with `angle:`; `polygon(6, d: 10.mm)` or `polygon(c, 6, d: 10.mm)`, regular (d/r through the corners; `fit: "sides"`: the circle the sides touch, `d` across the flats; `angle:` the direction of its first corner, else its first side lies at the bottom, horizontal); `slot(length, w)` (a stadium, length end to end along X; `angle:` turned, `center:` elsewhere) or `slot(p, q, w:)` (round two centres); `teardrop(r | d, angle:, flat:)` or `teardrop(c, r | d, …)` (see Printing).
  - Not sketch shapes: `polygon([vec(0, 0), vec(30, 0), vec(0, 20)])` (through the points; `smooth: true`, a smooth closed curve through them), `text("text", size: 10.mm, font: "Sans")` (starting at the origin on the baseline; `weight: "light"`, thin … black or 100 … 900, the nearest the font has installed; `bold: true`, `italic: true`, a style at the end of the font's name counting too, `"Sans Bold"`; `spacing: 1.mm` more between the letters, `lineSpacing: 1.5` times between the lines) and `load("outline.svg")` (see Importing parts).
  - `s.contains(p)`: whether point `p` lies inside a solid (on its surface: no), or inside a profile's area (`p`, a world point, taken onto the profile's plane); e.g. to choose the half of a cut that holds a point. A profile drawn on a face or lying in another plane gives its `bbox`, `spots` and `outline` where it lies, in world coordinates, as `contains` reads them.
  - A profile's parts: `p.outer` (the outline without its holes), `p.holes` (each hole filled, a Profile each), `p.pieces` (its separate regions, each with its holes).
  - Combine with `+ - &`: profiles overlap, add up and cut each other, where a sketch draws one outline; a sketch's `s.profile` is a Profile too, so the two mix (`s.profile - circle(d: 5.mm)`). Profiles move, turn, scale and mirror like solids: `p.move(x: 10.mm, y: 5.mm)`, `p.rotate(30.deg)` or `p.rotate(z: 30)` (in its plane, about the origin; `around: q` about a point), `p.scale(2)` or `p.scale(x: 2, y: 3)`, `p.mirror(X)` (across the line through the origin with that normal). `.round(r)` rounds the corners; `.offset(d)` grows (d > 0) or shrinks it (shrunk to nothing, an empty profile); `.area`. A difference that takes all of a profile is an empty profile too (`isEmpty`), still a Profile; extruding one is an error that says so. `p.across(X)` stands it up across X as `extrude(along: X)` does (its x along Y, its y up Z; `across(Y)`: its x along X): `loft([a.across(X), b.across(X).move(x: 20.mm)])` lofts along X.
  - `.extrude(h)` makes a solid along +Z (negative h goes down); options `shear: vec(dx, dy)` (the top moved that much sideways from the bottom, the sides leaning straight: an oblique prism), `taper: 3.deg` (the sides lean in going away from the profile, whichever way the solid goes: up, down with a negative height, along X or Y; staying flat and meeting at sharp edges: the outline narrows and the holes widen; a negative taper the other way; `h` is still the height along the axis, and an edge or hole of the profile that would close up before the top is an error), `symmetric: true` (half the height each side of the profile, which is the middle of the solid: a taper narrows both ways from it, a twist turns half each way), `twist: 90.deg` (the profile turns around Z as it rises, evenly: twisted vases, spiral columns; `twist: 2 * 360.deg` two turns; not with `taper`). `along: Y` stands the profile up across Y (its x along X, its y up Z) and pushes it towards +Y, `along: X` across X (its x along Y, its y up Z) towards +X; a negative height goes the other way: a prism along X or Y without turning anything. A profile lying in another plane, a section (`body.section(XZ.offset(10.mm)).extrude(2.mm)`), one turned or moved whole, or one drawn on a face, is extruded across its own plane, along its normal, from where it lies.
  - `.revolve()`: turned around the axis, standing up: the profile's x is the radius and its y the height along Z (pots, bottles, knobs). `.revolve(axis: X, angle: 180.deg)`: around an axis in the profile's plane (a direction through the origin or an `Axis`), without standing up; `angle:` turns less than all the way. A profile drawn on a face or plane, or lying in one (a section, one turned), turns where it lies, and its axis is a world one, as everything else in that plane (a direction through the plane's origin, an `Axis` anywhere): the half section of a lathe part drawn on XZ, as the Front view shows it, turns round Z with `revolve(axis: Z)`, or `revolve()`, which turns a profile standing upright round its own y axis.
  - On a face or plane, add or remove material in one step: `carlo().extrude(circle(d: 6.mm), on: frame, depth: 5.mm)` grows outwards along the frame's Z; `carlo().cut(circle(d: 6.mm), on: frame, depth: 2.mm)` digs in, `through: true` cuts all the way. The depth is always positive, the call saying which way (a negative one is an error: use the other call). Both accept `taper:`; `on:` also takes a face selector (`on: faces.top`) or a plane, and `at: vec(…)` a point, brought onto the face, where the profile's origin goes (`body.cut(circle(d: 3.mm), on: faces.top, at: vec(5.mm, 2.mm, 0.mm), depth: 2.mm)`); a solid in place of the profile is placed as it is, its z = 0 on the face and +Z out of it, no depth: `body.cut(hole(M3, 6.mm, "counterbore"), on: faces.top, at: vec(…))`.
  - Threads: `body.thread(face, "M8")` cuts a thread on a cylindrical face: on the outside of a shaft (made at the thread's nominal diameter, ⌀8) the grooves, on the wall of a hole (made at the tap drill, about ⌀6.8 for M8) the thread a screw fits. The size names the standard: ISO metric `"M8"` (coarse) or `"M8x1"` (fine), unified inch `"1/4-20 UNC"`, `"1/4 UNF"`, `"#10-32"`, trapezoidal for lead screws `"Tr12x3"`, ACME `"1/2-10 ACME"`, buttress `"S20x4"` (DIN 513), BSP pipe threads `"G1/2"` (parallel) and `"R1/2"` (tapered), `"1/2 NPT"` (tapered; the shaft is the pipe's outside diameter), Edison lamp bases `"E27"`, `"E14"`, bottle and jar necks `"28-400"` (SPI/GPI 400, 410, 415 from 13 to 120 mm), PET bottles `"PCO 1881"`, `"PCO 1810"`, and the garden hose `"3/4 GHT"`; which to use, and how to recognise one, under Threads: choosing one, recognising one. Tapered threads have their nominal size at the fixed end and narrow by 1 in 16 on the diameter towards the tip of a shaft, or into a hole. `taper: 1.79.deg` makes any thread conical the same way, the angle each side leans from the axis (R and NPT have 1.79°, 1 in 16; `taper: 0.deg` makes them parallel): a tapered metric plug, a conical thread that tightens as it goes in. `pitch: 1.mm` alone puts a 60° thread of that pitch on the cylinder's own diameter. The thread covers the whole face, or `length: 10.mm` or `turns: 8` from the free end (the tip of a shaft, the opening of a hole; `flip: true` the other end). `starts: 2` for multi-start threads, `left: true` left-handed (every thread is at the same angle at its free end: a shaft and a hole threaded from the same free end mesh, whatever their lengths, so a nut cut out of a tube threaded over a bolt's tip runs on it; the Examples menu's dual-thread bolt does so), `clearance: 0.2.mm` the play for printed parts (0.15 mm by default in holes, none on shafts), `chamfer: false` without the 45° bevel at the free end. In the 3D view, right-click a cylinder: **Thread** lists the sizes that fit it. Every thread is built exactly from its boundary (each corner of the profile on its own helix, on a cone for tapered ones, a ruled face between two of them; the profile repeated in a lead for more starts) and cut to the face: a second or less for an M8 × 25. The `threads` library (`threadedRod`, `tappedHole`) makes loose rods and tools to cut.
- Extrude and cut faces: `carlo().extrude(faces.top, depth: 5.mm)` sweeps flat faces of the body outwards along their normals and adds the material, `carlo().cut(faces.top, depth: 2.mm)` sinks them (a negative depth to extrude does the same). `along: vec(1, 0, 1)` sweeps them in another direction, slanted sides: material is added when the direction leaves the face, removed when it enters. In the 3D view: right-click a face, Extrude face… or Cut face….
- **Paths, sweeps and lofts:**
  - Paths (type `Path`): `path([vec(0, 0, 0), vec(0, 0, 20), vec(30, 0, 20)])` (straight segments, mitred corners; `closed: true`), `spline([…])` (a smooth curve through the points), `helix(r | d, pitch:, height:, left: false)` (around +Z, starting at (r, 0, 0)). Paths move, rotate and mirror like solids; `p.length` is how long one is, along it.
  - `path([…], bend: 5.mm)` rounds every corner with an arc of that radius, as a bent tube or wire: straight stretches and arcs of a known radius (unlike `spline`, curved all along); a corner whose sides are too short for its arc is an error naming it.
  - From a sketch: `s.path` is what the sketch draws (its lines, arcs, curves and circles that are not construction) as one path, open or closed, where the sketch lies; drawn with its constraints, so it follows them. A sketch drawing several separate chains gives them all in `s.paths` (in the order they are drawn), and `s.path` is then an error. Mind that `s.polyline` closes unless `closed: false`.
  - From a solid's edges: `body.path(edges.loop(faces.top))` joins the selected edges end to end (a bead along a rim, a groove round a lid); they must make one chain.
  - From two views: `path(top.path, front.path)` is the curve in space that, seen across the first path's plane, is the first, and across the second's, the second: draw a handle or a bent rod from above and from the front, each in its own sketch, and sweep along the result. The two must cover the same stretch along the line they share.
  - `profile.sweep(path)`: the profile, drawn on XY around the origin, starts at the beginning of the path, normal to it, with its +Y kept towards world +Z (towards +Y when the path starts vertically). `frenet: true` follows the curvature (use it for helices: springs, threads). `twist: 360.deg` turns the profile once around the path on the way, evenly along it (twisted ribbons, ropes; not with `frenet`). Holes in the profile give tubes.
  - How the profile turns about the path (its roll; it always stays across the path): by itself as little as it can, which after many bends in space leaves its +Y wherever it ends up. To decide it, give one of: `twist: t => 60.deg * sin(t * 720.deg)`, a function of how far along the path (0 at the start, 1 at the end) giving how far it has turned there (counted from the start: `t => …` at 0 is the profile as placed); `up: Z`, its +Y as close to that way as it can be all along (a road or a rail that does not bank; an error, with where, if the path runs that way somewhere, as a vertical stretch does for `up: Z`); `guide: rail`, another path, its +Y towards the point of the rail as far along it (halfway along the path, halfway along the rail): it works where `up` cannot, a path going up and over. Along a helix the profile keeps to its axis by itself (a square wire coils with its sides along the axis, over any number of turns), and a twist is counted from there. On a path with sharp corners (`path` without `bend:`) these work too: each stretch between corners is swept with its roll, and the stretches meet in the planes that halve the corners, mitred. A path that turns right back on itself cannot be swept along: an error says where.
  - `loft([circle(r: 20), rect(30).move(z: 40), circle(r: 10).move(z: 80)])`: a smooth solid through profiles placed in space; `ruled: true` gives flat sides; `along: path` blends them along that path (its centreline), each where it lies across it; `start: Z`, `end: Z` the directions it leaves the first profile and reaches the last (`weight:` how strongly, 1 by default). Profiles with holes are lofted as tubes when every profile has the same number of holes.
- **Constrained sketches** (2D, on XY or on a face): `auto s = sketch();` then add geometry and constraints and take `s.profile`.
  - Areas: the profile fills what lies inside an odd number of loops: a loop inside another is a hole, and where two loops overlap (two circles crossing) the overlap is a hole too. Where more than two lines or arcs meet at a point (a line across a rectangle from side to side, an arc from one corner to another; a line or arc ending on another between its ends splits it there), there are no simple loops: every area they close is full. `s.fill(at)` makes the area holding `at` full whatever the loops say, `s.fill(at, full: false)` empty (`at` a vector, or a point of the sketch, which keeps it in its area as the constraints move it; such a point, used by nothing else, does not count among the degrees of freedom; the last fill in an area counts). In the window the full areas are tinted, and the sketch bar's ◩ turns an area full or empty with a click inside it.
  - Construction geometry: `construction: true` on any geometry call or shape (`s.line(p, q, construction: true)`, `s.rect(…, construction: true)`) makes guides to constrain to, drawn dashed in the window, never part of the profile.
  - Geometry: `s.point(x, y)` (where it starts: constraints move it; `fixed: true` pins it there), `s.line(p, q)`, `s.arc(center, start, end)` (counter-clockwise; their points sketch points or vectors, which become new points: to join two lines, give the second the first one's `.end`), `s.circle(center, r: | d:)` (without r/d the radius is left to the constraints), `s.polyline([p1, p2, vec(…)], closed: true)` (returns the lines; vectors become new points), `s.ellipse(center, rx:, ry:, angle:)` (rx along its own x axis, `angle` from X, ry across; what is not given is left to the constraints, the turn too: `s.ellipse(c, rx: 20.mm, ry: 12.mm)` with c fixed leaves 1 degree of freedom), `s.spline([p1, p2, vec(…)], closed: false)` (a smooth curve through the points, in order, vectors becoming new points: open, its two ends join lines and arcs as theirs do; `closed: true` goes round back to the first point, a loop of its own; it bends evenly, as a thin strip bent through the points would, and its points move it: constrain them; `.points`, `.start`, `.end`, `.closed`, `.length` along the curve). `construction: true` geometry helps constraining but is not part of the outline.
  - Shapes, made of the geometry above with their constraints, the same shapes and arguments as the profiles above (the points they need are new; a vector where a point goes, here and in `s.circle` and `s.ellipse`, becomes a new point starting there; without the centre, `s.circle(d: 10.mm)`, `s.rect(40.mm, 20.mm)`, `s.polygon(6, d: 10.mm)`, `s.slot(30.mm, 6.mm)`, `s.teardrop(d: 5.mm)`, it is a new point at the origin, free to move): `s.rect(p, q)` (opposite corners), `s.rect(p, w:, h:)` (one corner, p the lower left) or `s.rect(center: c, w:, h:)` returns its 4 lines p → (q.x, p.y) → q → (p.x, q.y), that is bottom, right, top, left when p is the lower left corner; they are horizontal and vertical, so a rectangle of new corners has 4 degrees of freedom, 0 with w, h and a fixed centre (a construction diagonal holds the centre in its middle); `angle: 30.deg` turns it (its first side that far from X: the sides are then square to each other and parallel in pairs instead of horizontal and vertical), `angle: "free"` leaves the turn to the constraints (`s.parallel(r[0], line)` lays it along a slanted line); `corner: r` rounds the four corners. `s.polygon(center, n, r: | d:, fit:, angle:)` returns the n lines of a regular polygon, its corners on a construction circle of that radius (`fit: "corners"`, the default), or its sides touching it with `fit: "sides"` (`d` across the flats: a nut's spanner size); `angle` is the direction of the first corner from the centre, else the turn is left free (1 degree of freedom: `s.horizontal(lines[0])` takes it; it starts with the first side at the bottom, horizontal, where the profile has it); `s.polygon([p, q, vec(0, 20)])` is the closed polyline through the points. `s.slot(p, q, w:)` returns `[line, arc round q, line, arc round p]`: two half circles joined by lines tangent to them, 0 degrees of freedom with p, q fixed and w given; `s.slot(length, w, center: c, angle:)` the same by its length end to end, along X unless turned (a construction line joins the two centres, c in its middle). `s.teardrop(c, r: | d:, angle:, flat:)` returns `[arc, line, line]`: an arc round c and two lines tangent to it meeting above it, `angle` (45° unless given) from the vertical; `flat: true` cuts the point with a line touching the circle's top (`[arc, line, flat, line]`); 0 degrees of freedom with c fixed and r given. Sizes given (w, h, r, d, rx, ry, angle, corner: one dimension for the four corners) are dimensions, shown and editable in the sketch view (a slot's length is not: the dimension would be between its centres).
  - Constraints: `coincident(p, q)`, `fix(p)`, `horizontal(line | p, q)`, `vertical(…)`, `length(line, v)`, `distance(p, q, v)`, `distance(p, q, v, along: X | Y)`, `distance(p, line, v)`, `on(p, line | circle | arc)` (a shape's lines instead of p: every corner on the circle, the shape inscribed: `s.on(s.polygon(c, 6), circ)`), `parallel(a, b)`, `perpendicular(a, b)`, `angle(a, b, v)` (between the line directions, start → end), `equal(a, b)` (lengths or radii), `radius(c, v)`, `diameter(c, v)`, `tangent(line | circle, circle | line)` (a shape's lines and a circle: every side touching it, the shape round it: `s.tangent(s.rect(center: c), circ)`), `midpoint(p, line)`, `symmetric(p, q, line)`, `concentric(a, b)` (circles, arcs, ellipses or a point round the same centre), `angle(line, v)` (of one line from X).
  - On ellipses: `on(p, e)`, `tangent(line, e)`, `concentric(e, …)`, `radius(e, rx: v, ry: v)` (either or both), `horizontal(e)` / `vertical(e)` (its x axis along X or Y), `angle(e, v)`, and `equal(e)`: as wide as tall, a circle. A round ellipse looks the same however it is turned: its turn then stays where it is, unless an angle sets it, and is not a degree of freedom.
  - `s.fillet(p, r)` rounds the corner where two lines meet at p (r is shown as a dimension on its arc).
  - Reading back: `p.x`, `p.y`, `p.pos`, `line.start`, `line.end`, `line.length`, `line.mid`, `c.center`, `c.radius`, `e.center`, `e.rx`, `e.ry`, `e.angle`, `s.dof` (degrees of freedom left; conflicting constraints are an error naming them), `s.solved`.
  - `s.profile` solves and returns the closed loops of non-construction lines, arcs, circles and ellipses as a `Profile` (inner loops are holes). Lines, arcs and curves with a free end (open) stay in the sketch, drawn, but out of the profile, with a warning naming them. Under-constrained sketches still work, with a warning listing the lines of the free points; conflicting constraints are an error pointing at them.
  - **On a face:** `auto s = carlo().sketch(faces.top);` draws on that flat face, with the axes of `carlo().frame(faces.top)` (origin at the face's centre; on a wall x to the right and y up seen from outside; `origin:` and `x:` as frame takes them). The face's edges are in the sketch from the start, as references: fixed construction geometry, no degree of freedom, shown in the sketch view. `s.edges` lists them, each loop from its lowest edge counter-clockwise like a rect's sides (bottom, right, top, left), the outside first; `s.origin` is the origin as a fixed point; `s.project(edges.…)` flattens other edges of the solid onto the plane as references (a hole's rim under the face; a circle seen aslant becomes an ellipse). Constrain to them as to any geometry: `s.distance(c.center, s.edges[0], 5.mm)`, `s.concentric(c, s.project(edges.filter(…))[0])`. `sketch(frame)` and `sketch(plane)` draw on a frame or plane, with `s.origin` and no edges.
  - The profile of such a sketch lies where it was drawn: `carlo().cut(s.profile, depth: 2.mm)` and `carlo().extrude(s.profile, depth: 1.mm)` need no `on:`, `s.profile.extrude(3.mm)` stands on the face, `revolve` turns it there and `loft` goes through profiles drawn on different planes. Moved, offset, tiled, hulled or combined with a profile of no place it stays in its plane (in the sketch's coordinates); profiles lying in one plane (a sketch's, a section, one moved up) combine, two in different planes are an error.
- **Transforms:** `move(v | x:, y:, z:)`, `rotate(x:, y:, z:)` or `rotate(angle, axis:)` (a direction through the origin, or an `Axis` anywhere), `scale(k)` or `scale(x: 2, y: 0.5, z: 1)` (a factor each: an ellipsoid from a sphere; the faces become freeform; `around: p` keeps point p where it is instead of the origin), `mirror(X)` (plane through the origin with that normal) or `mirror(plane)` (any plane), `color(c)`.
- **Placement:** `a.nextTo(b, X, gap: 10.mm)` (beside `b` that way, only its x changing; an oblique direction like `vec(1, 2, 0)` puts its centre on the line from `b`'s centre that way, the boxes touching, `gap` further along it), `a.on(b)`, `a.align(b, x: "center", z: "min")` (each axis `"min"`, `"center"` or `"max"` of the bounding boxes).
- **Patterns:** `hole.linearPattern(4, step: vec(10, 0, 0))` (a grid with `n2: 3, step2: vec(0, 10, 0)`), `peg.pathPattern(path, n: 8)` (along a path, each copy turned as it turns; `rotate: false` only moves them), `peg.circularPattern(6, axis: Z, angle: 360.deg)` give one solid with all the copies (subtract it to cut them all).
- **Axes:** `axis(origin: vec(10, 0, 0), direction: Z)`, `axis(p1, p2)` (through two points), `carlo().axis(edges.filter(…))` (the line of a straight edge, or the centre and normal of a circular one such as a hole rim), `shaft.axis(faces.largest)` (the axis of a cylinder's, a cone's or a turned face), `frame.axis(X)` (an axis of a frame). Fields: `origin`, `direction`. Use them with `rotate(angle, axis: a)` and `circularPattern(n, axis: a)`.
- **Surfaces** (type `Surface`: faces with an edge open, no inside):
  - Made by sweeping a curve instead of a profile: `path([vec(-8.mm, 0), vec(8.mm, 0)]).sweep(route)` (the curve drawn on XY around the origin, as a profile is, placed across the path in the same way: a ribbon through the middle of anything swept along that path), or by lofting through paths: `loft([path1, path2])` (`ruled: true` for flat strips).
  - `body.split(surface)`: the pieces the surface cuts the solid into (it must reach across it), sorted as `split(plane)` sorts them; `pieces.push(from: surface, by: 3.mm)` moves each away from the surface, across it where it is nearest. A tube split lengthwise and opened: `tube.split(ribbon).push(from: ribbon, by: 3.mm)`, the ribbon swept along the tube's own path.
  - `fill(rim)`: a smooth face closing a closed path, a Surface; `through: [vec(…)]` points it passes through too (a dome); on a solid, `body.fill(edges.…, tangent: faces.…)` closes a loop of its edges (an opening, a cavity's rim), meeting the faces given smoothly. Thickened, it is a lid that follows the rim; sewn, it closes an open sheet.
  - `surface.thicken(2.mm)`: a solid that thick, on the side its normals point (negative: the other side); a surface lofted through closed paths (a square to a circle) whose sharp and smooth edges meet is thickened from its paths instead, each offset in its own plane, outwards for a positive thickness (the wall then that thick across the paths' planes).
  - `sew([sides, bottom, top])`: surfaces (and flat profiles for their ends) that close round a space, joined into one solid; when they leave a gap, the error says how many edges stay open.
  - A part cannot be a surface (it has no inside), and surfaces do not combine with `+ - &`: split, thicken or sew them.
- **Planes:** `XY` (its normal +Z, up), `XZ` (−Y, towards the front) and `YZ` (+X, to the right): each faces the way the Top, Front and Right views look at it, so a sketch on one reads as that view shows it, x to the right and y up; `plane(origin: vec(0, 0, 10), normal: Z)`, `plane(p1, p2, p3)` (three points; the normal follows p1 → p2 → p3 by the right-hand rule), `plane(axis, point)` (containing a line and a point), or the plane of a face: `carlo().plane(faces.top)`, or halfway between two parallel faces: `body.plane(faces.top, faces.bottom)` (the first one's normal). Planes also mirror: `s.mirror(plane)`.
  - `p.offset(5.mm)` is the parallel plane moved along the normal (negative goes the other way); `p.flip` reverses the normal.
  - Fields: `origin`, `normal`.
- **Frames** (an origin and X, Y, Z axes) to build on faces and planes:
  - `carlo().frame(faces.top)`: origin at the face centre, Z along the outward normal. On a wall (any face that is not flat) X is horizontal and to the right seen from outside and Y goes up, on every side: a text reads and a teardrop points up whichever wall it is on; on a flat face X is the global X. The same axes place profiles with `on:`. Options: `origin: vec(…)` (projected on the face), `x: Y`.
  - `plane.frame(origin: vec(…), x: …)`: on a plane the origin defaults to the plane's origin; give a point to choose another one.
  - `World` is the global frame; `f.at(x: 10, y: -5)` moves the origin in local coordinates; `f.turn(30.deg)` rotates X and Y around Z. Fields: `origin`, `x`, `y`, `z`.
  - `solid.placeOn(f)`: a solid built on XY with Z up is moved onto the frame. A plane works too (`placeOn(plane)`): its origin is the zero, with the axes of a frame on a face. A boss: `cylinder(d: 8, h: 5).placeOn(f)`; a pocket: `carlo() - box(10, 10, 3).move(z: -3).placeOn(f)`.
  - `solid.placeOn(f, from: faces.bottom)` lays a face of the solid against the frame instead (the face's middle on its origin, the two facing each other, X on X); `at: vec(…)` carries that point of the face instead of its middle. A lid on a vase's mouth, wherever the vase leans: `lid.placeOn(vase().frame(faces.farthest(Z)), from: faces.bottom)`; turn it with `frame.turn(30.deg)`. Place on… in the window writes these.
- **Cutting:** `s.halves(plane)` returns the two sides of the cut, each one solid: `.above` (where the normal points) and `.below`. `s.split(plane)` returns the pieces the cut leaves, both sides, as a `Solid[]` ordered along X, then Y, then Z: more than two when the plane crosses a slot; choose among them with `.above(plane)`, `.below(plane)`, `.largest`… or make a part of each with `@parts`.
- **Textures and noise:** `noise(x, y, z, seed: 3)` is smooth noise, about -1…1 with features about one unit across (lengths count in mm); `loopNoise(around, along, bumps: 6)` is noise round a loop, `around` 0…1 once round, with no seam where it closes. Both take `kind:`: `"cells"` (0 at the point each cell grows from, about 1 farthest from it), `"edges"` (0 on the borders between the cells: a Voronoi relief on any surface), `"ridged"` (1 on sharp ridges), each 0…1; and `octaves:` (up to 8), finer and weaker layers added on top for a rougher, more natural texture. `profile.outline(n, round: 2.mm)` gives n points evenly round a profile's outline, each with `.at`, its outward `.normal` (turning round a corner as on a fillet `round` big, so that a push inwards smaller than that does not cross itself) and `.around` (0…1). `polygon(points, smooth: true)` is a smooth closed curve through the points, filled. `loft` also takes rings of points (`Vec3[][]`, the same count in each): one smooth surface through every point, closed round each ring, the end rings filled flat, in milliseconds where a loft through as many smooth profiles takes seconds; `loft(rings, inside: innerRings)` makes it hollow, the inner wall through the inner rings, a floor at the inner first ring and a flat rim between the last rings, which lie in one plane. Together they make textured solids: a ring per height, every outline point pushed along its normal by a function of where it is, lofted; along a curve, `path.frames(n)` gives n frames evenly along it, Z along the path and turning as little as they can, to place the rings on with `placeOn` (see `examples/03_randomvase.hcad`, a vase along a curve with its lid):
  ```d
  Vec3[] ring(double up)
  {
      Vec3[] pts;
      foreach (q; circle(r: 30.mm).outline(140, round: 2.mm))
      {
          auto p = q.at + q.normal * (2.mm * loopNoise(q.around, up * 8, bumps: 9));
          pts ~= vec(p.x, p.y, 100.mm * up);
      }
      return pts;
  }
  // then: Vec3[][] rings; foreach (k; 0 .. 41) rings ~= [ring(k / 40.0)]; return loft(rings);
  ```
- **Profiles on curved faces:** `body.cut(profile, wrap: faces.largest, depth: 1.mm)` and `body.extrude(profile, wrap: …, depth:)` lay a flat profile on one face of any shape, rolled onto it like a label on a bottle: lengths are kept along the face, exactly on cylinders, cones and extrusions, nearly on lofts and revolved shapes (stretched a little where the face swells away from the line through the anchor), stretched on a sphere. The profile's x runs across the face (round a cylinder), its y along it, read from outside (on a hole's wall, from inside it); its origin goes to the front of the face (the side facing -Y, halfway along) or to `at:`, a point over it. `project: faces.…` carries it along a direction instead (`along:`, else the face's normal at that point), from the plane touching the face there, as a light casts it: stretched where the face turns away, for a logo on the front of a ball. The edges are curves on the face, not a mesh; text, tilings and sketches all work. Except on a cylinder (where everything is carried exactly), a curve shorter than 0.6 mm, a small rounding, is laid as its chord. Pockets and reliefs wholly inside the face are built at once, the face holed and the floors sewn in, with no boolean: a hundred regions on a vase in a second or two; so are cuts through a wall whose other side is the face moved in (a shelled cup, a tube: both faces holed, the sides between). Regions crossing the face's edges (a tiling's cells cut at its rim, a letter over it), or cuts into other faces, take the boolean way, slower on curved freeform faces (seconds for dozens of regions); only those: the regions wholly inside are still built at once.
- **Knurling:** `body.knurl(faces.largest, kind: "diamond" | "straight" | "diagonal", pitch: 1.6.mm, depth: 0.5.mm, angle: 30.deg, margin: 0.5.mm)` raises a grip on a face of any shape (a knob, a handle, a slider's pad, the side of a lofted grip), laid on it as `wrap:` lays a profile: diamonds, ridges along the face or leaning ones, `margin` in from its edges; round a face that closes on itself (a cylinder, a loft through rings) a whole number round, so it closes too; built on the face with no boolean.
- **Tilings:** `region.tiles(kind: "hex", size: 10.mm, gap: 2.mm)` fills a profile with cells `gap` apart, as one profile: subtract it for a grille (`plate - region.tiles(…)`), or cut or extrude it on a face for pockets or reliefs (`body.extrude(r.tiles(…), on: faces.top, depth: 1.mm, taper: 30.deg)`, slanted sides). Kinds: `"square"`, `"hex"`, `"triangle"`, `"brick"`, `"octagon"` (with small squares between), `"diamond"`, `size` the distance between neighbouring cells' centres; `"voronoi"`, cells round points scattered about `size` apart (`jitter:` 0, hexagons, to 1, the default; `relax:` passes that even them out; `seed:`), or round `points:` of your own. Your own tile: `tile:` a profile or a list of them (a sketch's profile, say), repeated by `step: [a, b]`; the copies (shrunk by the gap) must not overlap, and an error says which two do. Cells crossing the region's border are cut there, `whole: true` keeps only those wholly inside. With no gap (the default) the cells touch, and are joined into one area. A region drawn on a face or lying in another plane (a section) is tiled in that plane, and the tiles stay there (`body.cut(cells, depth: 1.mm)` needs no `on:`). `round:` rounds each cell, `angle:` turns the tiling, `origin:` puts a cell there (else at the region's centre). `scale:` a factor for each cell and `keep:` which cells stay, as functions of the cell's centre: `scale: (Vec2 c) => 1 - c.length / 80.mm` grades the holes, `keep: (Vec2 c) => noise(c.x / 20, c.y / 20) > 0` leaves some out. A region on a curved surface takes a noise texture instead (`kind: "edges"`).
- **Separate bodies:** `s.pieces` lists the disconnected bodies of a solid (e.g. after a cut through it), ordered by position along X, then Y, then Z; pick one with `[i]` or sort them (`s.pieces.sort((a, b) => a.volume > b.volume)`). A list of solids also says which are where: `.above(plane)` and `.below(plane)` (by centre of mass, so the pieces of a split, which touch the plane, count), `.crossing(plane)` (those it cuts through), `.nearest(point)`, `.largest`, `.smallest`, and `.top`, `.bottom`, `.left`, `.right`, `.front`, `.back` (the highest, lowest…): `carlo().split(cutPlane).below(cutPlane).largest`. To make parts of them, see `@parts`.
- **Push and pull:** `s.push(from: ref, by: 5.mm)` moves a solid away from a point, a Plane or an Axis, `s.pull(to: ref, by: 5.mm)` towards it, along the line from the reference to the solid's centre of mass (from a plane along its normal, from an axis square to it). On a list each solid goes its own way, so the pieces of a cut spread apart, an exploded view: `carlo().split(cutPlane).push(from: cutPlane, by: 4.mm)`. A solid whose centre is on the reference stays, with a warning.
- **Importing parts:** `load("part.stl")`, `load("part.obj")`, `load("part.ply")`, `load("part.3mf")`, `load("part.glb")` (or `.gltf`), `load("part.step")`, with `scale:` (STL, OBJ and PLY are read in mm; 3MF uses its own unit and build transforms; glTF its nodes' transforms, from metres to mm and turned from Y up to Z up, not compressed with Draco or meshopt). A mesh that is not quite a solid, as scans often are, loads with `repair: true`: triangles doubled facing each other (walls of no thickness) are taken out and, where the surface touches itself along an edge or at a vertex, the sheets are parted; holes are left, and the error says what remains. Meshes become solids (coplanar triangles merged into faces, closed meshes only), STEP files keep their exact geometry; both can be cut, filleted, measured and selected like any other solid. Paths are relative to the model file and must stay inside the project directory. To remodel a mesh exactly, set it straight first if it came tilted (`load("part.stl").aligned` lies on its largest flat face, longest along X, centred in X and Y and resting on z = 0); `writeln(load("part.stl").features)` lists what it is made of (flat faces, holes and shafts with the ISO size they match, cones, spheres, roundings, chamfers with their size, surfaces turned round an axis, patterns of holes, with plausible sizes; `hcad features part.stl` on the command line, `hcad_features` for agents); load it as a see-through reference part to compare. `hcad section part.stl --plane xy --at 3` (`hcad_section` for agents) gives a cut across it as lines, arcs and circles with their sizes, and as a sketch ready to paste and extrude. `clone.deviation(original)` is how far apart the two surfaces are at most (`assert(clone.deviation(original) < 0.2.mm)` in a unittest); `hcad compare model.hcad --a clone --b original -o map.png` (`hcad_compare`) also gives the mean, the share within a tolerance, a picture of the clone coloured green where it matches, yellow at the tolerance, red beyond, and the patches of each surface the other does not follow (area, offset, facing: a missing chamfer or countersink shows there). `hcad diff` lists the pieces of material to add or cut, the thin differences apart, and the section that shows each piece; `hcad scan file.stl --axis z` the holes and pockets met along an axis with their shapes and depths; `hcad section … --compare` draws two sections on each other and `--projection` reads a shadow's outline; `hcad fit model.hcad --a clone --b original --param width` tunes @param lengths until the two match (and says when the shape, not the sizes, differs); `hcad match` matches the operations of the two one by one (a nut trap cut in steps is one hole); `hcad section … --region u0,v0,u1,v1` keeps the outlines inside a rectangle of the plane (a lettering); `hcad literals model.hcad --original original` lists the numbers the model repeats and which sizes of the original they are, to name them as @params once the copy matches. `hcad review model.hcad --a clone --b original -o review.png` (`hcad_review`) runs the whole comparison round in one: distances both ways, material, drawings outside and of the voids, and close-ups of the first entries of each, framed where they are in sight; `--look x,y,z` adds a close-up of what is at that point. The reports of compare, diff, lines and match are numbered: `--focus 2 -o close.png` (`focus: 2`) draws a close-up of entry 2, from where it is in sight (what lies in front cut away when nothing is); `hcad render … --from right --look-at 1,2,13 --size 14 --opaque -o detail.png` (`view`, `opaque` for agents) takes a picture from anywhere, close on a detail, and compare and lines take the same `--from`, `--look-at`, `--size`, `--cut`.
